item.research_question: How do sintering temperature and dwell time during spark plasma sintering (SPS) influence the densification behavior, microstructural evolution (specifically grain growth), and mechanical properties of Cantor-type high-entropy alloys?
item.processing_route: Spark plasma sintering (SPS) using a RACS25 hybrid device; cylindrical samples (Ø10 × 5 mm) sintered under 50 MPa uniaxial pressure; temperature range 875–1100 °C in 25 °C increments; dwell times of 3 min or 5 min; direct loading into graphite POCO EDM-1 dies without prior compaction
item.test_conditions: Room temperature static uniaxial compression tests at a strain rate of 8 × 10⁻³ s⁻¹ up to 50% permanent strain; Vickers hardness testing (HV0.1 and HV1); Archimedes density measurement; SEM and EDS microstructural analysis
key_findings: Maximum relative densities were achieved at 1050 °C/3 min and 1100 °C/3 min, showing a non-linear relationship between temperature and densification.
The highest compressive strength of 1888 MPa was obtained for samples sintered at 1070 °C for 5 min.
Samples sintered at 1050 °C/3 min and 1060 °C/5 min exhibited compressive strengths of 1879 MPa and 1861 MPa, respectively.
The lowest compressive strength of 1702 MPa was recorded for the sample sintered at 1100 °C/3 min.
Average grain sizes ranged from 8.74 μm (at 1060 °C/5 min) to 10.59 μm (at 1080 °C/5 min), with abnormal local grain growth reaching up to 114.27 μm at 1080 °C.
All sintered samples retained a single-phase FCC structure with homogeneous elemental distribution and no detectable phase segregation or secondary precipitates.
Vickers hardness values remained consistent across conditions, ranging between 167–175 HV0.1 and 169–172 HV1, with the optimal sample reaching 180 HV1.
item.mechanism: The authors argue that while SPS is rapid, grain boundary migration is kinetically constrained by short dwell times, yet elevated temperatures and longer holds promote significant grain growth, particularly when no precipitates exist to inhibit it. They attribute the non-linear densification to local thermo-electrical effects causing overheating at grain boundaries, which can lead to localized melting or vaporization, while the high compressive strength at moderate temperatures correlates with a refined microstructure and maintained grain boundary cohesion.
item.limitations: The authors note that the exact temperature at grain boundaries is unknown, making precise control difficult, and that the use of graphite dies causes carbon diffusion leading to a brittle surface layer and local chromium depletion requiring sandblasting.
item.future_work: The authors state that further microstructural investigations are necessary to precisely determine the relationships between sintering parameters and densification mechanisms, and that the findings are relevant for designing HEA components for demanding applications.
quotes: The results reveal a non-linear relationship between sintering temperature and densification, with maximum relative densities obtained at 1050 °C and 1100 °C for short dwell times.
The highest compressive strength was observed for the samples sintered at 1070 °C (1888 MPa), followed closely by those sintered at 1050 °C (1879 MPa) and 1060 °C (1861 MPa).

System: Cantor-type high-entropy alloy (CoCrFeMnNi) prealloyed powder. Processing: Spark plasma sintering (SPS) using a RACS25 hybrid device; cylindrical samples (Ø10 × 5 mm) sintered under 50 MPa uniaxial pressure; temperature range 875–1100 °C in 25 °C increments; dwell times of 3 min or 5 min; direct loading into graphite POCO EDM-1 dies without prior compaction. They attribute the non-linear densification to local thermo-electrical effects causing overheating at grain boundaries, which can lead to localized melting or vaporization, while the high compressive strength at moderate temperatures correlates with a refined microstructure and maintained grain boundary cohesion..
